items.prompt: Nobody at Northfield Ledger ever added `case-fold` to `package.json`. Why does it still count as part of their software supply chain?
choices: It doesn't — only direct dependencies count as supply chain risk
It's a transitive dependency: `ledger-pdf` (a package Northfield did choose) depends on it, and npm installs it automatically
It only counts once a CVE is published for it
It only counts if it's listed explicitly in a `security.txt` file
items.explanation: The supply chain includes everything that ends up running in your build or your app, not just what you typed into `package.json` yourself. `case-fold` reached Northfield because `ledger-pdf` (a direct, deliberately-chosen dependency) depends on it, and npm resolves and installs the whole tree automatically — nobody had to individually approve `case-fold` for it to end up running code in CI.
items.reference:
package.json (reviewed) → ledger-pdf (reviewed) → case-fold (never seen by anyone at Northfield)

Why: trust flows down the tree automatically — review only happens at the top.

items.prompt: A typical modern app has a handful of direct dependencies and hundreds or thousands of transitive ones. What does that ratio imply about how much of the app's dependency tree was ever individually reviewed?
choices: All of it — package managers require every transitive dependency to be manually approved
Only the small handful of direct dependencies were deliberately chosen; the rest arrived automatically, unreviewed
None of it — direct dependencies aren't reviewed either, since installing is automatic
Exactly half, since transitive dependencies alternate with direct ones in the tree
items.explanation: The handful of direct dependencies are the ones a team actually decided to bring in — they're at least nominally reviewed at adoption time. Everything transitive was pulled in as a side effect of that decision, by whoever maintains the direct dependency, with no review step from the app's own team at all. That imbalance — few reviewed, many not — is the actual attack surface this unit is about.
items.reference:
package.json (reviewed) → ledger-pdf (reviewed) → case-fold (never seen by anyone at Northfield)

Why: trust flows down the tree automatically — review only happens at the top.

items.prompt: Why does 'I trust `ledger-pdf`' effectively become 'I trust whatever `ledger-pdf` trusts' once it's installed?
choices: It doesn't — trust never propagates between packages
Because `npm install` resolves and runs the entire dependency tree, so anything `ledger-pdf` depends on gets the same install-time execution privileges as `ledger-pdf` itself
Only if `ledger-pdf` is explicitly marked as 'trusted' in its own package.json
Because npm asks for manual confirmation before installing any transitive dependency
items.explanation: There's no separate, lower trust tier for transitive dependencies — once npm resolves the tree, every package in it, direct or transitive, gets installed and can run install scripts with the same privileges. Choosing `ledger-pdf` implicitly extends the same level of trust to everything it depends on, whether or not anyone at Northfield ever reads that list.
items.reference:
package.json (reviewed) → ledger-pdf (reviewed) → case-fold (never seen by anyone at Northfield)

Why: trust flows down the tree automatically — review only happens at the top.

items.prompt: A burned-out solo maintainer hands off publish access to a volunteer who had been filing helpful PRs for weeks; the volunteer then ships a version with a malicious payload under the package's real, existing name. Which attack pattern is this?
choices: Typosquatting
Maintainer takeover
Dependency confusion
Compromised CI/build pipeline
items.explanation: This is maintainer takeover — the attacker doesn't need a fake name or a resolver misconfiguration, because they gained legitimate publish rights to the real, already-trusted package. The install history, the reputation, and the existing user base all transfer directly to the malicious version, which is exactly what makes it so effective and hard to catch by name alone.
items.reference:
🤝 Maintainer takeover

real package, real name, new bad actor

🔤 Typosquatting

fake package, similar name

Why: each pattern exploits a different kind of trust — a name's reputation, a resolver's precedence, or a maintainer's own access.

items.prompt: An attacker publishes a package called `reqeusts` (note the swapped letters), hoping developers fat-finger the popular `requests` library's name. Which attack pattern is this?
choices: Maintainer takeover
Compromised CI/build pipeline
Typosquatting
Dependency confusion
items.explanation: This is typosquatting: a deliberately similar (but not identical) package name, banking on a fat-fingered install command borrowing the real package's reputation by proximity of spelling rather than by compromising the real package at all.
items.reference:
🤝 Maintainer takeover

real package, real name, new bad actor

🔤 Typosquatting

fake package, similar name

Why: each pattern exploits a different kind of trust — a name's reputation, a resolver's precedence, or a maintainer's own access.

items.prompt: A company has an internal package `acme-auth-lib` on a private registry. An attacker publishes a same-named package with a higher version number on the public registry, and a misconfigured resolver installs the public (malicious) one instead. Which attack pattern is this?
choices: Typosquatting
Dependency confusion
Maintainer takeover
Compromised CI/build pipeline
items.explanation: This is dependency confusion — it exploits how a package resolver picks between an internal and public registry (often 'highest version wins'), not a similar-looking name or stolen publish access. The malicious package doesn't need to look like anything special; it just needs to share the exact internal name and outrank it on version number.
items.reference:
🤝 Maintainer takeover

real package, real name, new bad actor

🔤 Typosquatting

fake package, similar name

Why: each pattern exploits a different kind of trust — a name's reputation, a resolver's precedence, or a maintainer's own access.

items.prompt: Which defense specifically protects against a registry or mirror silently serving different bytes than what you installed before, under the same version number?
choices: Dependency scanning
Lockfile integrity hashes
An SBOM
Pinning a version range
items.explanation: An integrity hash in the lockfile records a cryptographic fingerprint of the exact bytes that were installed. If a later install fetches different bytes under the same name and version — from a compromised mirror, a man-in-the-middle, or any tampering — the hash won't match and the install can be aborted. Scanning and SBOMs are about knowing what's in your tree; integrity hashes are about whether what you got is what you expected.
items.reference:
DefenseProtects against
Lockfile integrity hashDifferent bytes served under the same version
SBOMNot knowing what's actually shipped
ScanningKnown, already-disclosed CVEs
Pinning + reviewA trusted package's next release going bad

Why: each defense closes a different gap — none of them substitutes for the others.

items.prompt: Which defense specifically answers 'is package X anywhere in what we've already shipped,' even for artifacts built months ago?
choices: Pinning a version range
An SBOM (kept on file per released artifact)
Lockfile integrity hashes
A `.gitignore` entry
items.explanation: An SBOM is an inventory of what's actually in a specific built artifact, generated at build time and kept on file. That's what lets the question 'is package X anywhere in anything we've shipped' become a lookup across stored SBOMs instead of a manual repo-by-repo search — and it stays answerable long after the build, since the SBOM doesn't expire when the build finishes.
items.reference:
DefenseProtects against
Lockfile integrity hashDifferent bytes served under the same version
SBOMNot knowing what's actually shipped
ScanningKnown, already-disclosed CVEs
Pinning + reviewA trusted package's next release going bad

Why: each defense closes a different gap — none of them substitutes for the others.

items.prompt: Which defense is specifically limited to catching versions with a *known, already-disclosed* vulnerability — and would have said nothing about `case-fold` v2.4.1 on day one?
choices: Pinning + version-bump review
Lockfile integrity hashes
Dependency / CVE scanning
An SBOM
items.explanation: Scanning works by matching your dependency tree against a database of already-published vulnerabilities — it can only flag a version once someone has reported and published an advisory for it. A brand-new malicious release with no CVE yet passes a scan cleanly, which is exactly why `npm audit` stayed green through all eleven days of Northfield's incident.
items.reference:
DefenseProtects against
Lockfile integrity hashDifferent bytes served under the same version
SBOMNot knowing what's actually shipped
ScanningKnown, already-disclosed CVEs
Pinning + reviewA trusted package's next release going bad

Why: each defense closes a different gap — none of them substitutes for the others.

items.prompt: How does this unit's territory differ from `security/secrets-management`'s?
choices: They're the same topic under two different names
Secrets-management is about your own credentials leaking from your own code; this unit is about third-party code you didn't write being the thing that leaks them
Secrets-management only applies to frontend apps, this unit only applies to backend apps
This unit is a stricter version of secrets-management with more rules
items.explanation: Secrets-management's Mira hardcodes her own team's database password into her own code — the leak originates entirely inside code Northfield's own engineers wrote. `case-fold`'s postinstall script scraping CI environment variables originates from code nobody at Northfield wrote, reviewed, or even knew existed. Both incidents can result in leaked credentials, but the trust boundary that failed is completely different.
items.reference:
Secrets-management: your code leaks your secret
Supply chain: someone else's code leaks it, and you never reviewed that code

Why: the failure point determines which defenses actually apply.

items.prompt: `case-fold`'s postinstall script exfiltrated AWS credentials from CI's environment variables — the same *kind* of value secrets-management covers. Why doesn't that make this the same unit?
choices: It doesn't matter what leaked — the leaking mechanism is what defines the unit's scope, and here it's a third-party dependency, not the app's own code
It does make it the same unit, and the two should be merged
AWS credentials are out of scope for secrets-management entirely
Supply-chain incidents never actually involve credentials leaking
items.explanation: The *value* that leaked (an AWS credential) is the same category secrets-management discusses, but *how* it leaked is what actually determines which defenses would have helped: rotation and scanning your own git history (secrets-management) wouldn't have stopped `case-fold`'s postinstall script — only supply-chain defenses (integrity checks, `--ignore-scripts`, dependency review) address a leak that originates from a dependency's own code running automatically.
items.reference:
Secrets-management: your code leaks your secret
Supply chain: someone else's code leaks it, and you never reviewed that code

Why: the failure point determines which defenses actually apply.

items.prompt: A routine-looking patch version bump adds a new `postinstall` script that wasn't there before. Why is that specific addition worth treating as a red flag, more than most other diff lines?
choices: It isn't — postinstall scripts are purely cosmetic and can't run meaningful code
A postinstall script runs automatically during `npm install`, with no separate approval step, before any of your own code ever executes
It's only a concern if the package is older than five years
Postinstall scripts only run in production, never in CI
items.explanation: Most code in a dependency only runs when your app actually imports and calls it — a postinstall script runs unconditionally, automatically, the moment `npm install` finishes, regardless of whether the package's exported functions are ever used. That makes a newly-added postinstall script one of the loudest possible signals in a version-bump diff: new code that executes with no gate at all.
items.reference:
npm install → postinstall runs automatically → your own app code hasn't executed yet

Why: a script that runs at install time bypasses every gate your own code would otherwise pass through first.

items.prompt: `case-fold` v2.4.1's exfiltration payload ran on 'every single CI run' for eleven days, not just once. Why did a single malicious version keep re-triggering the same payload repeatedly?
choices: It didn't — the payload only ran once, the first time the package was installed anywhere
Every CI job runs `npm install` fresh (or restores a cache and re-runs install), so the postinstall script executes again on every single run until the version is removed or blocked
The payload replicated itself into other packages after the first run
CI jobs only run install scripts on Mondays by default
items.explanation: CI environments are typically ephemeral or frequently rebuilt — each job that runs `npm install` (or `npm ci`) against a lockfile pinning the compromised version re-executes that version's postinstall script from scratch. There's no 'already ran once, skip it next time' behavior; the exposure window is every single install across every job, for as long as the compromised version stays in the lockfile.
items.reference:
npm install → postinstall runs automatically → your own app code hasn't executed yet

Why: a script that runs at install time bypasses every gate your own code would otherwise pass through first.

items.prompt: In the L2 mermaid diagram, `case-fold` sits two hops away from Northfield's own `package.json`. Why does that specific depth matter for whether anyone would notice it in a code review?
choices: Depth doesn't matter — every dependency, at any depth, shows up identically in a pull-request diff

A PR that bumps `ledger-pdf` shows a diff for `ledger-pdf` itself, not for what `ledger-pdf` depends on — a reviewer would have to deliberately dig into the lockfile's full tree to even see `case-fold`'s name
Depth only matters for packages published more than a year ago
Two hops is shallow enough that npm automatically flags it as risky
items.explanation: A typical code review looks at the diff for the thing that actually changed — 'bump ledger-pdf from 3.1.3 to 3.1.4.' Nothing about that diff surfaces `case-fold`'s version or its new postinstall script unless the reviewer specifically opens the full lockfile and traces the tree by hand. The deeper a compromised package sits, the less likely ordinary review practices ever put it in front of a human.
items.reference:
package.json (depth 0) → ledger-pdf (depth 1, reviewed on bump) → case-fold (depth 2, invisible to that same review)

Why: review naturally focuses on what changed at the top of a diff, not on everything that change quietly drags in underneath.

items.prompt: The L2 diagram shows every arrow — install, postinstall execution, the outbound POST — as individually unremarkable. What does that imply about detecting this kind of compromise by looking for 'suspicious' individual actions?
choices: Nothing unusual is needed to detect it — each step already looks like an obvious attack in isolation

No single step looks anomalous on its own; the compromise is only visible when you ask a different question, like 'what's actually in our dependency tree' or 'did this version add a new install script'
The compromise can only be detected by disabling npm entirely
Each arrow is individually blocked by default in modern npm versions
items.explanation: npm running an install script is documented, expected behavior. A library depending on a formatting helper is unremarkable. An HTTP POST from a CI job isn't inherently suspicious either, in isolation. None of the individual steps trip a conventional 'this looks like an attack' alarm — which is exactly why the defenses that catch this class of incident (SBOM inventories, integrity checks, version-bump review) work by asking structural questions about the dependency tree itself, not by looking for anomalous-looking individual actions.
items.reference:
package.json (depth 0) → ledger-pdf (depth 1, reviewed on bump) → case-fold (depth 2, invisible to that same review)

Why: review naturally focuses on what changed at the top of a diff, not on everything that change quietly drags in underneath.

items.prompt: L2 says Northfield's trust in `case-fold` is 'the sum of every decision along the chain,' not a decision anyone made about `case-fold` specifically. What does that framing imply about who is actually responsible for reviewing a transitive dependency?
choices: Nobody is responsible — transitive dependencies fall outside anyone's job by definition

In practice, no single person ever explicitly takes on that responsibility unless a team deliberately builds a process (SBOMs, scanning, version-bump review) that surfaces transitive dependencies for review
The maintainer of `case-fold` is fully responsible for Northfield's production security
Only Northfield's legal team is responsible, since it's a contractual matter
items.explanation: Without a deliberate process, transitive-dependency review falls into a gap: it's nobody's specific job by default, because normal review habits (reading a PR diff) naturally stop at the layer that actually changed. The defense stack exists precisely to close that gap — an SBOM, a scanner, or a version-bump policy assigns 'notice what's in the full tree' to a process instead of leaving it to whichever engineer happens to think to look.
items.reference:
package.json (depth 0) → ledger-pdf (depth 1, reviewed on bump) → case-fold (depth 2, invisible to that same review)

Why: review naturally focuses on what changed at the top of a diff, not on everything that change quietly drags in underneath.

items.prompt: `npm audit` stayed clean throughout Northfield's eleven-day incident. What class of compromise does audit-style CVE scanning structurally fail to catch, regardless of how often it's run?
choices: Any compromise involving a package published in the last decade
A brand-new malicious version of a package that has no disclosed CVE or advisory yet — scanning can only match against vulnerabilities someone has already reported
Compromises that only affect development environments, never CI
Nothing — audit-style scanning catches every kind of supply-chain compromise if run frequently enough
items.explanation: A CVE database entry has to exist before a scanner can match anything against it, which means there's always a lag between 'a malicious version is published' and 'a scanner would flag it' — and that lag can be arbitrarily long if nobody reports it. Running the scan more frequently doesn't close this gap; it's a structural limit of the approach, not a tuning problem.
items.reference:
Scanner checks: is this version already known bad?
case-fold 2.4.1: brand new, zero prior reports → scan passes clean

Why: scanning defends against known-bad versions, not against a trusted package's very next release.

items.prompt: If Northfield had run `npm audit` on an hourly schedule instead of occasionally, would that have caught `case-fold` v2.4.1 any sooner during the eleven-day window?
choices: Yes — more frequent scans always catch supply-chain compromises faster
No — audit results depend on when an advisory gets published for that version, not on how often the scan itself runs; running it more often just re-checks the same (still empty) database faster
Yes, but only if the scan also included a manual code review step
No, because `npm audit` doesn't work on CI systems at all
items.explanation: Increasing scan frequency only helps once a matching advisory exists to be found — before that, every scan run (hourly or daily) queries the same database and gets the same clean result, because there's genuinely nothing to match yet. This is exactly why pinning and version-bump review exist as a separate layer: they don't wait for an external advisory at all, they scrutinize the change itself at the moment it's proposed.
items.reference:
Scanner checks: is this version already known bad?
case-fold 2.4.1: brand new, zero prior reports → scan passes clean

Why: scanning defends against known-bad versions, not against a trusted package's very next release.

items.prompt: Given that scanning can't catch a brand-new malicious version, what does it actually contribute to the overall defense stack?
choices: Nothing — since it missed this incident, scanning has no real value
It closes a real, different gap: catching packages that stayed unpatched after a vulnerability *was* disclosed — a common and separate failure mode from a zero-day maintainer takeover
Scanning only matters for packages with more than 1 million downloads
Scanning replaces the need for lockfiles entirely
items.explanation: 'Scanning doesn't catch zero-day maintainer takeovers' isn't the same as 'scanning is useless' — a large share of real-world incidents are teams running known-vulnerable versions for months after a fix already exists, which is precisely what scanning is built to catch quickly. The defense stack works by combining tools with different blind spots, not by finding one tool that covers everything.
items.reference:
Scanner checks: is this version already known bad?
case-fold 2.4.1: brand new, zero prior reports → scan passes clean

Why: scanning defends against known-bad versions, not against a trusted package's very next release.

items.prompt: A developer runs `npm install case-fold@latest` and commits the resulting lockfile change, unknowingly pulling in the malicious v2.4.1. Does the lockfile's integrity-hash mechanism catch this?
choices: Yes — the integrity hash always flags a malicious package regardless of how it entered the lockfile
No — the integrity hash only verifies that installed bytes match what the lockfile *already records*; it faithfully records whatever version was resolved at update time, malicious or not
Yes, but only on the second install after the first one
No, because integrity hashes are only checked for direct dependencies, never transitive ones
items.explanation: An integrity hash answers 'do these bytes match what my lockfile says they should be' — it says nothing about whether the lockfile *itself* was updated to point at something malicious. When the developer ran the update and committed it, the lockfile now faithfully records v2.4.1's hash as the expected one; every future install matches perfectly, because it's matching against a record that already includes the compromise.
items.reference:
Lockfile pins: exact version + integrity hash
Protects: install-time tampering (different bytes than recorded)
Doesn't protect: the lockfile being updated to point at something bad in the first place

Why: a lockfile locks in whatever you point it at — it doesn't judge whether that target is safe.

items.prompt: What are the two distinct jobs a lockfile's `integrity` field and version-pinning together actually do?
choices: Encrypt the package contents, and enforce a minimum team size for review
Pin the exact resolved version (no silent drift on install), and verify the installed bytes match a recorded hash (no tampering in transit)
Automatically patch known vulnerabilities, and notify the maintainer of every install
Prevent any new dependency from ever being added without a security team's sign-off
items.explanation: These are the two concrete jobs described in L2: pinning gives you the same exact version on every install (not 'whatever the current `^2.3.0` resolves to today'), and the integrity hash detects if the bytes served for that exact version ever differ from what was recorded before — e.g. a compromised mirror serving something different under the same version number.
items.reference:
Lockfile pins: exact version + integrity hash
Protects: install-time tampering (different bytes than recorded)
Doesn't protect: the lockfile being updated to point at something bad in the first place

Why: a lockfile locks in whatever you point it at — it doesn't judge whether that target is safe.

items.prompt: Two teammates both run `npm ci` (install strictly from the lockfile) weeks apart, without anyone touching `package.json` or the lockfile in between. What guarantees that they both end up with the exact same `case-fold` version and bytes?
choices: Nothing guarantees it — `npm ci` re-resolves version ranges fresh every time
The lockfile's recorded exact version plus its integrity hash together guarantee it: same version requested, and the hash check confirms the bytes match too
Only running on the same operating system guarantees it
npm caches results globally across all users, which is what guarantees consistency
items.explanation: `npm ci` is specifically designed to install strictly from the lockfile without re-resolving ranges, so both teammates request the exact same pinned version; the integrity hash then confirms the bytes they each received match the recorded fingerprint. Together, that's what makes 'reproducible install' a real guarantee rather than a hope — as long as nobody has updated the lockfile to point at something new in between.
items.reference:
Lockfile pins: exact version + integrity hash
Protects: install-time tampering (different bytes than recorded)
Doesn't protect: the lockfile being updated to point at something bad in the first place

Why: a lockfile locks in whatever you point it at — it doesn't judge whether that target is safe.

items.prompt: An SBOM is generated once, at build time, for a release shipped six months ago. A new CVE for a package in that release gets published today. Is the six-month-old SBOM still useful?
choices: No — an SBOM expires and must be regenerated before it can be scanned again
Yes — the SBOM is a static inventory of what was actually in that artifact, so it can be re-scanned against today's advisory database at any time, without rebuilding anything
Only if the artifact is still actively deployed in production
No — SBOMs only cover direct dependencies, never the transitive ones a CVE would target
items.explanation: The SBOM doesn't need to be regenerated to stay useful — it's a factual record of what was in that specific build, and 'is package X, version Y anywhere in this record' is a question you can ask against it at any later point, against whatever advisory database exists at query time. That's the dashed feedback arrow in L2's pipeline diagram: new advisories flow back and get checked against every SBOM you've kept, not just the newest one.
items.reference:
SBOM generated once, at build time → stays a valid queryable record indefinitely → re-scanned whenever a new advisory is published

Why: scanning is a standing query against stored SBOMs, not a one-time gate that only matters at release.

items.prompt: Why do regulators and enterprise customers increasingly ask vendors for an SBOM as a contract requirement, rather than just asking 'is your software secure'?
choices: Because an SBOM is a legal document that guarantees zero vulnerabilities
Because an SBOM lets the customer independently re-run their own vulnerability query against a vendor's actual inventory, instead of only trusting the vendor's word after the fact
Because SBOMs are required by international shipping law
Because an SBOM replaces the need for any security testing on the vendor's side
items.explanation: 'Is your software secure' is a question the vendor could just assert an answer to. An SBOM turns it into something the customer can check for themselves against whatever advisory feed they trust, whenever they want — including for a new CVE published long after the vendor last looked. That independence, not any legal guarantee, is what makes an SBOM a meaningfully different ask than a verbal assurance.
items.reference:
SBOM generated once, at build time → stays a valid queryable record indefinitely → re-scanned whenever a new advisory is published

Why: scanning is a standing query against stored SBOMs, not a one-time gate that only matters at release.

items.prompt: A team pins every dependency to an exact version (no `^` or `~` anywhere) but never actually looks at what changed before merging a version-bump PR. Does exact pinning alone prevent a `case-fold`-style incident?
choices: Yes — exact pinning by itself is sufficient protection against any malicious version
No — pinning only stops *automatic* drift; a human still has to approve the bump, and without review, that approval can happen on autopilot for a bump that adds a new postinstall script
Yes, but only for packages published in the last 30 days
No, because exact pinning is incompatible with using a lockfile at all
items.explanation: Exact pinning removes the silent, automatic path to a new version — no install can drift to it without someone explicitly editing `package.json`. But 'someone explicitly bumped it' and 'someone actually looked at what changed' are different things; a team that pins everything but rubber-stamps every bump PR is still exposed to exactly the same incident, just with an extra approval click added.
items.reference:
Pinning alone

stops silent drift, not a rubber-stamped bump

Pinning + review

a bump requires a diff AND someone actually reading it

Why: the technical stack makes the information visible — a team still has to decide to look at it.

items.prompt: What specific signal in a version-bump diff should a minimal-version-review policy treat as the loudest possible red flag?
choices: Any change to the changelog's wording
A newly added install script (`postinstall`/`preinstall`), since it means new code that runs automatically before the app's own code ever executes
A version number that increases by more than one minor version
A package that has been downloaded fewer than 1,000 times total
items.explanation: Most changes in a dependency bump are inert until your code actually calls into the new version. A newly added install script is categorically different — it runs unconditionally at install time, which is exactly the mechanism `case-fold` used. That specific kind of diff line deserves scrutiny out of proportion to how small it looks.
items.reference:
Pinning alone

stops silent drift, not a rubber-stamped bump

Pinning + review

a bump requires a diff AND someone actually reading it

Why: the technical stack makes the information visible — a team still has to decide to look at it.

items.prompt: Using the provided `simpleHash(str)` function (a stand-in for the real SHA-512 a lockfile actually uses), implement `verifyIntegrity(content, expectedHash)` — return `true` if `simpleHash(content)` equals `expectedHash`, `false` otherwise.

tests.description: returns true when content matches the expected hash
returns false when content doesn't match
works for empty content too

items.explanation: This mirrors L3's `verifyIntegrity` over a real SHA-512 comparison: a lockfile records an expected hash, and an install-time check re-hashes the actual bytes received and compares. `simpleHash` here stands in for a real cryptographic hash (which needs `node:crypto`, unavailable in this sandbox) — the comparison logic, which is the actual point of the exercise, is identical either way.
items.reference:
lockfile says: expectedHash
install fetches: actual bytes → hash them → compare

Why: a mismatch means the registry served different bytes than what was recorded last time — the exact tampering an integrity check is built to catch.

items.prompt: Using the provided `simpleHash(str)` function, implement `findTampered(packages)` where `packages` is an array of `{ name, content, expectedHash }` objects. Return an array of the `name`s whose `content` does NOT match its `expectedHash`, in the same order they appear.

tests.description: returns empty array when everything matches
flags a single tampered package
tests.expr: expect(findTampered([{ name: 'a', content: 'foo', expectedHash: simpleHash('foo') }, { name: 'case-fold', content: 'malicious-payload', expectedHash: simpleHash('clean-original') }])).toEqual(['case-fold'])

tests.description: preserves order and can flag multiple
tests.expr: expect(findTampered([{ name: 'x', content: 'bad', expectedHash: simpleHash('good') }, { name: 'y', content: 'ok', expectedHash: simpleHash('ok') }, { name: 'z', content: 'bad2', expectedHash: simpleHash('good2') }])).toEqual(['x', 'z'])

items.explanation: This is the batch version of the same check — a CI step that verifies every package in `node_modules` at once, rather than one at a time, and reports exactly which names failed so the failure is actionable instead of a single opaque 'integrity check failed' message.
items.reference:
lockfile says: expectedHash
install fetches: actual bytes → hash them → compare

Why: a mismatch means the registry served different bytes than what was recorded last time — the exact tampering an integrity check is built to catch.

items.prompt: Using the provided `simpleHash(str)` function, implement `allIntact(packages)` where `packages` is an array of `{ name, content, expectedHash }`. Return `true` only if every package's content matches its expectedHash; `false` if even one doesn't.

tests.description: returns true when everything matches
tests.expr: expect(allIntact([{ name: 'a', content: 'foo', expectedHash: simpleHash('foo') }, { name: 'b', content: 'bar', expectedHash: simpleHash('bar') }])).toBe(true)

tests.description: returns false when one package is tampered
tests.expr: expect(allIntact([{ name: 'a', content: 'foo', expectedHash: simpleHash('foo') }, { name: 'case-fold', content: 'bad', expectedHash: simpleHash('good') }])).toBe(false)

tests.description: returns true for an empty package list

items.explanation: This is the gate a CI pipeline actually needs before deciding whether to proceed: not the list of which packages failed (that's `findTampered`'s job), just a single yes/no answer to 'is it safe to continue the build' — which is exactly what `--ignore-scripts` followed by an integrity check, as shown in L3's CI YAML, is deciding before allowing `npm rebuild` to run any install scripts at all.
items.reference:
lockfile says: expectedHash
install fetches: actual bytes → hash them → compare

Why: a mismatch means the registry served different bytes than what was recorded last time — the exact tampering an integrity check is built to catch.

items.prompt: Implement `isLooseRange(range)` matching L3's `LOOSE_RANGE` pattern: return `true` if `range` starts with `^` or `~`, is exactly `'*'`, or is an empty string `''`. Return `false` for an exact version like `'2.3.0'`.

tests.description: caret range is loose
tilde range is loose
exact version is not loose
wildcard is loose

items.explanation: This is L3's `LOOSE_RANGE` regex applied directly: any range that lets `npm install` silently pick a newer version without a `package.json` edit counts as loose. `case-fold`'s `^2.0.0` range in Northfield's tree matched this exact pattern — it's what allowed the malicious 2.4.1 to be picked up automatically.
items.reference:
/^[\^~]|^\*$|^$/

Why: a loose range means a fresh install can drift to a new version with no diff to review — the exact gap pinning closes.

items.prompt: Using the provided `isLooseRange(range)` helper, implement `findLooseRanges(node, depth)` matching L3's tree walker: given a tree node `{ name, range, resolved, dependencies: [] }`, return a flat array of `{ name, range, resolved, depth }` for every node (at any depth) whose range is loose. The root call starts at `depth = 0`; `range: null` (the root app itself) should never be flagged.

tests.description: flags a loose transitive dependency at the correct depth
tests.expr: expect(findLooseRanges({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [{ name: 'ledger-pdf', range: '^3.1.0', resolved: '3.1.4', dependencies: [{ name: 'case-fold', range: '^2.0.0', resolved: '2.4.1', dependencies: [] }] }] })).toEqual([{ name: 'ledger-pdf', range: '^3.1.0', resolved: '3.1.4', depth: 1 }, { name: 'case-fold', range: '^2.0.0', resolved: '2.4.1', depth: 2 }])

tests.description: does not flag an exactly-pinned dependency
tests.expr: expect(findLooseRanges({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [{ name: 'font-metrics', range: '1.2.0', resolved: '1.2.0', dependencies: [] }] })).toEqual([])

tests.description: root node itself is never flagged
tests.expr: expect(findLooseRanges({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [] })).toEqual([])

items.explanation: This is L3's full tree walker: a recursive traversal that reports a loose range at whatever depth it actually occurs, which is exactly what surfaces `case-fold` at depth 2 even though nobody at Northfield wrote its range themselves — `ledger-pdf`'s own `package.json` did.
items.reference:
/^[\^~]|^\*$|^$/

Why: a loose range means a fresh install can drift to a new version with no diff to review — the exact gap pinning closes.

items.prompt: Using the provided `isLooseRange(range)` helper, implement `countPinnedVsLoose(node)` that walks a dependency tree (same shape as before) and returns `{ pinned, loose }` — the total count of non-root nodes with an exact version versus a loose range, across the whole tree.

tests.description: counts a mix of pinned and loose dependencies
tests.expr: expect(countPinnedVsLoose({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [{ name: 'ledger-pdf', range: '^3.1.0', resolved: '3.1.4', dependencies: [{ name: 'case-fold', range: '^2.0.0', resolved: '2.4.1', dependencies: [] }, { name: 'font-metrics', range: '1.2.0', resolved: '1.2.0', dependencies: [] }] }] })).toEqual({ pinned: 1, loose: 2 })

tests.description: returns zero counts for a tree with only the root
tests.expr: expect(countPinnedVsLoose({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [] })).toEqual({ pinned: 0, loose: 0 })

tests.description: counts an all-pinned tree correctly
tests.expr: expect(countPinnedVsLoose({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [{ name: 'a', range: '1.0.0', resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [] }, { name: 'b', range: '2.0.0', resolved: '2.0.0', dependencies: [] }] })).toEqual({ pinned: 2, loose: 0 })

items.explanation: This is the summary-level view a team would actually want on a dashboard: not every individual loose dependency's name, but a single ratio answering 'roughly how exposed is our tree to silent version drift' — useful for tracking whether a pinning policy is actually improving over time.

items.prompt: Implement `toPurl(name, version)` that returns a package URL string in the form `pkg:npm/<name>@<version>`, matching L3's SBOM generator's `purl` field.

tests.description: builds a purl for a simple package
builds a purl for a different package
handles a scoped-looking name literally

items.explanation: A `purl` (package URL) is the standard, machine-readable identifier CycloneDX and SPDX both use to name a component unambiguously across ecosystems — it's a small formatting detail, but it's what lets an SBOM scanner match components against an advisory database reliably instead of matching on loose name/version string pairs.
items.reference:
{ name: 'case-fold', version: '2.4.1' } → 'pkg:npm/case-fold@2.4.1'

Why: an SBOM's value comes from being a complete, structured inventory — not a partial or approximate one.

items.prompt: Implement `flattenComponents(node)` that walks a dependency tree (`{ name, range, resolved, dependencies: [] }`) and returns a flat array of `{ name, version }` for every dependency node — skip the root itself (identified by `range === null`).

tests.description: flattens a nested tree, excluding the root
tests.expr: expect(flattenComponents({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [{ name: 'ledger-pdf', range: '^3.1.0', resolved: '3.1.4', dependencies: [{ name: 'case-fold', range: '^2.0.0', resolved: '2.4.1', dependencies: [] }] }] })).toEqual([{ name: 'ledger-pdf', version: '3.1.4' }, { name: 'case-fold', version: '2.4.1' }])

tests.description: returns an empty array for a tree with only the root
tests.expr: expect(flattenComponents({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [] })).toEqual([])

tests.description: handles siblings at the same depth
tests.expr: expect(flattenComponents({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [{ name: 'a', range: '1.0.0', resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [] }, { name: 'b', range: '2.0.0', resolved: '2.0.0', dependencies: [] }] })).toEqual([{ name: 'a', version: '1.0.0' }, { name: 'b', version: '2.0.0' }])

items.explanation: This is the structural core of L3's `generateSBOM` — turning a nested tree into the flat `components` list a CycloneDX document actually needs, regardless of how deep any given dependency sits. Depth is exactly what a code-review diff loses and an SBOM preserves.
items.reference:
{ name: 'case-fold', version: '2.4.1' } → 'pkg:npm/case-fold@2.4.1'

Why: an SBOM's value comes from being a complete, structured inventory — not a partial or approximate one.

items.prompt: Using the provided `toPurl` and `flattenComponents` helpers, implement `generateSBOM(node, appName, appVersion)` returning `{ bomFormat: 'CycloneDX', specVersion: '1.5', metadata: { component: { name: appName, version: appVersion } }, components }`, where each entry in `components` is `{ type: 'library', name, version, purl }`.

tests.description: produces the correct top-level shape and metadata
tests.expr: expect((() => { const s = generateSBOM({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [] }, 'northfield-ledger-app', '1.0.0'); return { bomFormat: s.bomFormat, specVersion: s.specVersion, metadata: s.metadata }; })()).toEqual({ bomFormat: 'CycloneDX', specVersion: '1.5', metadata: { component: { name: 'northfield-ledger-app', version: '1.0.0' } } })

tests.description: builds a full component entry with type and purl
tests.expr: expect(generateSBOM({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [{ name: 'case-fold', range: '^2.0.0', resolved: '2.4.1', dependencies: [] }] }, 'app', '1.0.0').components).toEqual([{ type: 'library', name: 'case-fold', version: '2.4.1', purl: 'pkg:npm/case-fold@2.4.1' }])

tests.description: components is empty for a tree with only the root
tests.expr: expect(generateSBOM({ name: 'app', range: null, resolved: '1.0.0', dependencies: [] }, 'app', '1.0.0').components).toEqual([])

items.explanation: This assembles the full SBOM document exactly as L3's `generateSBOM` does — a minimal but structurally real CycloneDX shape. Real tooling (cyclonedx-npm, syft) adds licenses and cryptographic hashes on top, but this is the core that makes 'is package X anywhere in this artifact' a lookup instead of a manual search.

items.prompt: Implement `scanSBOM(components, advisories)` matching L3's `scanSBOM`, where `components` is an array of `{ name, version, ... }` and `advisories` is an object mapping a package name to an array of known-bad versions. Return the subset of `components` whose `version` appears in `advisories[name]`, in the same order.

tests.description: flags a component matching a known-bad version
does not flag a clean version of a known package
ignores a package with no advisory entry at all

items.explanation: This is L3's worked-example scan against a stand-in advisory database — the exact query Priya's team couldn't run in minutes on day one, because no SBOM existed yet to run it against. Once an SBOM exists, this is a single filter call, not a manual audit.
items.reference:
advisories: { 'case-fold': ['2.4.1', '2.4.2'] }
components: [{ name: 'case-fold', version: '2.4.1' }] → flagged

Why: this is exactly the pipeline's dashed feedback arrow — a new advisory re-checked against every SBOM already on file.

items.prompt: Using the provided `scanSBOM` helper, implement `hasCriticalFinding(components, advisories)` that returns `true` if `scanSBOM` would return any findings at all, `false` if the scan is clean — matching the `--fail-on-critical` gate from L3's CI YAML.

tests.description: returns true when a component matches an advisory
returns false when the scan is clean
returns false for an empty component list

items.explanation: This is the pass/fail signal a CI pipeline actually branches on — `scanSBOM`'s full list of findings is useful for a human-readable report, but a build gate just needs a boolean to decide whether to block the release, exactly as `--fail-on-critical` does in L3's GitHub Actions step.

items.prompt: Implement `levenshtein(a, b)`, the classic edit-distance algorithm: the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or substitutions to turn string `a` into string `b`.

tests.description: distance between identical strings is 0
one substitution apart
two transpositions apart (like a typosquat)

items.explanation: This is L3's `levenshtein` implementation — a standard dynamic-programming table where each cell represents the edit distance between prefixes of `a` and `b`. It's the core primitive the typosquat detector builds on: a small edit distance from a well-known name is exactly the shape a typosquat takes.
items.reference:
'csae-fold' vs 'case-fold' → distance 2 (two transposed letters) → flagged as suspiciously close

Why: this catches lookalike names, not compromised real packages — a different attack pattern from case-fold's own incident.

items.prompt: Using the provided `levenshtein` helper, implement `findTyposquatCandidates(candidateName, popularPackages, maxDistance)` matching L3's version: return an array of `{ name, distance }` for every entry in `popularPackages` that is NOT identical to `candidateName` but is within `maxDistance` edits of it, sorted by ascending distance.

tests.description: flags a close lookalike name
does not flag the exact same name against itself
excludes names further than maxDistance

items.explanation: This is L3's full typosquat detector: it checks a candidate package name against a curated list of well-known names and flags anything suspiciously close but not identical. As the Checkpoint right after this code discusses, this detector catches lookalike-name attacks specifically — it would have flagged nothing for `case-fold` itself, since the real incident used the correct, legitimate name.
items.reference:
'csae-fold' vs 'case-fold' → distance 2 (two transposed letters) → flagged as suspiciously close

Why: this catches lookalike names, not compromised real packages — a different attack pattern from case-fold's own incident.

items.prompt: Using the provided `levenshtein` helper, implement `isSuspiciouslyClose(name, popularNames, maxDistance)` — a simpler boolean check than the full candidate list: return `true` if `name` is within `maxDistance` edits of ANY entry in `popularNames` (and isn't identical to it), `false` otherwise.

tests.description: returns true for a close lookalike
returns false for the exact real name
returns false when nothing is close enough

items.explanation: This is the fast-path version a `pre-install` hook would actually call — a single boolean gate ('block or warn on this install') rather than the full ranked list, useful when the only decision that matters is whether to interrupt the install at all.
